# What Nim is and why

Nim is often pitched in one line: it reads like Python and runs like C. That line is true, but it
explains nothing. A more useful description: Nim is a compiled, statically typed language, and the
result is a single binary that runs without a virtual machine.

This chapter shows what those two properties mean in practice. We start with the smallest program,
watch what happens when the code is wrong, and then weigh when Nim is worth choosing.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can explain what "compiled" and "statically typed" mean, run your first Nim
program, and read the type error the compiler prints.
:::

## Compiled, not interpreted

A Python program is read and executed line by line by an interpreter. A Nim program is translated
first. The compiler reads a `.nim` file, produces C code, and then calls a C compiler to build a
binary. That binary is what runs.

Three consequences follow:

- Mistakes are found before the program runs, not when the bad line is finally executed.
- The program runs as fast as C, because it becomes C.
- The result is a single file you can copy to another machine without installing Nim there.

The cost: every change needs a recompile. For small programs, that is a matter of seconds. As a
program grows, the difference gets more expensive: a bug that only appears in production costs far
more than one caught before the program runs.

## The first program

The examples in this chapter run with `nim`. If it is not installed yet,
[Installing Nim](installation.qmd) shows how; the examples are readable without running anything.

Save the following as `hello.nim`, then run `nim r hello.nim`.

```{.nim}
echo "Hello, Nim"
```

```{.txt}
Hello, Nim
```

`echo` writes its arguments to stdout and ends the line. There is no `main`, no semicolons, and
indentation defines the blocks. A single file may hold top-level statements like this one.

## Types are checked before the program runs

This is the difference from Python. In Nim, every value has a type the compiler already knows. When
the types do not match, the program never runs. Try this.

```{.nim}
var age: int = "twenty"
echo age
```

The compiler rejects it:

```{.txt}
main.nim(1, 16) Error: type mismatch: got 'string' for '"twenty"' but expected 'int'
```

Read it from left to right:

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `main.nim` | the file with the problem |
| `(1, 16)` | line 1, column 16 |
| `Error` | severity; the build stops here |
| `got 'string' ... but expected 'int'` | the value is a `string`, but an `int` is required |

There is no output, because no program runs. To a beginner this feels like an obstacle. Over time it
becomes an advantage: the same mistake in Python surfaces only when that line executes, perhaps
after real user data has arrived.

## Procedures and loops

Nim stays compact as programs grow. A procedure is written with `proc`, and the last expression in
its body becomes the return value.

```{.nim}
proc greet(name: string): string =
  "Hello, " & name

echo greet("Nim")
```

```{.txt}
Hello, Nim
```

`&` joins two strings. The line `"Hello, " & name` is the last expression, so it is what gets
returned. No `return` is needed as long as there is no branch.

Loops use the same indentation:

```{.nim}
var total = 0
for n in 1..5:
  total += n
echo total
```

```{.txt}
15
```

`1..5` is an inclusive range: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The `+=` operator adds to the existing value. `total`
uses `var` because its value changes; the chapter on [variables](variables.qmd) covers the choice
between `var`, `let`, and `const` in full.

## One codebase, many targets

The default backend is C. C++, Objective-C, and JavaScript backends are also available. The command
`nim c --backend:js hello.nim` produces a JavaScript file from the same code. For most programs we
rarely pick a backend by hand.

Nim 2.x uses ORC as its default memory management. ORC counts references and collects cycles, and
destructors run when a value leaves its scope. No garbage collector stops the whole program to
sweep memory. For everyday code, what matters is this: we never call `free`, and forgetting to
release memory is not a fatal mistake.

Nim also has *templates* and *macros*: code that runs at compile time to produce other code. That is
why Nim can offer domain-specific syntax and thin boilerplate without giving up performance. We will
meet them much later, since both need a firmer grasp of types first.

## When Nim fits, and when it does not

Nim fits when you need a native binary, predictable memory use, and readable code. Command-line
tools, network services, data processors, and programs shipped as a single file all qualify.

Nim is not the first choice when the ecosystem decides. For machine learning, Python libraries are
far more complete. For web work with the most job openings, JavaScript and Go are safer bets. Being
honest about this is more useful than selling one language as the answer to everything.

## Exercises

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

1. Change the `hello` program above so it prints your name instead of `Nim`.
2. In the addition example, change `1..5` to `1..10`. Predict the output before running it.
3. Write a program that prints `7 * 6` together with its result. Save it as `multiply.nim`.
4. The code `var age: int = "twenty"` fails to compile. Explain why the compiler points at column
   16, and not at column 5 where the name `age` sits.
5. Without running it, decide whether `echo greet(42)` on the `greet` example is valid. Explain your
   reasoning.

## Summary

- Nim compiles to C and then to a binary; no virtual machine runs while the program executes.
- Types are checked at compile time, so a type error stops the build before any output.
- `echo` writes to stdout; a procedure uses `proc` with its last expression as the return value.
- The backend can be swapped (C, C++, Objective-C, JavaScript); the default memory manager is ORC.
- Nim's ecosystem is smaller than Python's or JavaScript's; choose Nim for a need, not a trend.
